title: Why the Sound stays cold in July
teaches: Salt and density, the two-layer exchange over the sills, renewal at neap tides, upwelling, and the salt wedge at a river mouth
summary: **Salt makes water heavy.** Sea water in the Sound is about 2 to 3 percent denser than river water, far more than any change of temperature makes, so salt sets the layers.
**The Sound runs as two layers.** Fresher water flows out toward the Strait on top, and salty ocean water flows in underneath to replace the salt it carries away.
**A little river water drives a lot of exchange.** Each cubic metre of river water draws in something like twenty of ocean water below.
**The sills stir the layers.** Tidal currents over the shallow rise at Admiralty Inlet churn the water over it top to bottom, and much of the water leaving on top is mixed down and carried back in.
**Deep water is renewed at neap tides.** When the tide is weak, less fresh water is mixed into the inflow, so it is dense enough to sink to the bottom of the Main Basin.
**The sills also make internal waves.** Slow, tall waves on the boundary between the layers, which show on a calm surface as bands of smooth slicks.
**The summer inflow is cold.** Northerly winds on the outer coast bring cold deep water up along the shore, and that water feeds the Strait's deep inflow.
**Stirring spreads the sun's heat through the whole depth.** That, with the cold supply, keeps the Main Basin near 12 to 14 °C in summer, while shallow South Sound inlets reach 18 to 20 °C.
**A salt wedge belongs to a narrow river mouth.** Where little stirs the layers, salt water creeps upstream along the bottom until the river's flow holds it back.
**The Ballard Locks catch the salt before it reaches Lake Union.** Salt water let through by each opening slides along the canal bed, where a barrier and a drain catch most of it.

blocks.text: On a hot afternoon in late July, wade into Lake Washington at Madison Park and the water is warm enough to swim in for an hour; lesson 6 found its surface above 20 °C. Drive fifteen minutes west to Golden Gardens or Alki and walk into the Sound, and your ankles ache. The water there is about 12 or 13 °C. The same sun shines on both, through the same air, and the Sound has had all of May, June and July to warm up.

Lesson 6 explained a lake that stays cold at the bottom: warm water floats on cold, the layers hold apart all summer, and the sun's heat stays near the top, so the surface gets warm. The Sound is cold right up to the surface. Something takes the summer's heat away, or brings cold water in to replace it, or both.

The first good look at the Sound's depths came from the United States Exploring Expedition under Lieutenant Charles Wilkes, whose boats spent the summer of 1841 charting the Sound with the lead line, a weight on a marked rope dropped to the bottom.[^wilkes] Their charts, and every chart since, show a sea far deeper than a river valley: long basins more than 200 metres deep in places, each cut off from the next by a shallower rise in the floor at its entrance. Those rises, the **sills** of lesson 11, and the deep water behind them, are where the answer lies.

Lesson 6 built the idea of **density**, how much a given volume of water weighs, from temperature: cold fresh water is heavier than warm, so it sinks. Salt does the same job, and does it far more strongly. Water in the Sound holds about 30 grams of dissolved salt in every kilogram, a little less than the open ocean's 35. That salt makes it about 2 to 3 percent denser than river water: a cubic metre of Sound water weighs about 1,023 kilograms, a cubic metre of river water about 1,000.

Two or three percent sounds small until you compare it with temperature. Warming fresh water from 4 °C to 20 °C makes it less than 0.2 percent lighter.[^density] So in the Sound salt decides which water floats and which sinks, and temperature has only a small say. Unlike in the lake, a layer of fresher river water will float on salty water even when the river water is the colder of the two.

**In the kitchen.** Fill a clear glass halfway with tap water. In a cup, stir two teaspoons of salt into half a cup (about 120 millilitres) of water and add a few drops of food colouring. Pour the coloured salt water very slowly down the side of the glass, or through a straw held to the bottom. It slides under the tap water and stays there as a layer, with a sharp boundary you can see through the side.

Rivers pour fresh water into the Sound all year: the Skagit, by far the largest, then the Snohomish, the Puyallup, the Nisqually and dozens more. That water is light, so it spreads over the surface and flows seaward on top, out through Admiralty Inlet toward the Strait of Juan de Fuca. On the way it mixes with the salt water beneath and carries some of that salt out with it.

Salt is leaving the Sound all the time, then, yet the Sound stays salty. Something must bring the salt back. It is ocean water, flowing in along the bottom, under the outgoing layer, from the Strait. This is the **two-layer exchange**: fresher water out on top, salty water in below, one on top of the other and moving in opposite directions, while the tide sloshes both back and forth twice a day. Any place where river water meets and mixes with sea water is an **estuary**. The Sound is one on a grand scale; a river mouth such as the Duwamish's, later in this lesson, is a small one.

**An estimate** of how much ocean water the river water draws in. Salt is neither made nor lost, so the salt carried in below must equal the salt carried out on top. Measurements in the Main Basin give typical salinities of about 31 grams per kilogram in the deep water and 29.5 near the surface. Call the inflow *Q* and the river flow *R*. The outflow is the inflow plus the river water mixed into it, *Q* + *R*. Salt in: *Q* × 31. Salt out: (*Q* + *R*) × 29.5. Setting them equal gives *Q* × 1.5 = *R* × 29.5, so *Q* is about 20 times *R*.[^knudsen] The answer leans hard on the small difference between the two salinities: with 30.5 in place of 31 it would be about 30. Either way, a modest river flow drives an exchange tens of times larger.

The biggest river of all doesn't enter the Sound. The Fraser, which drains much of interior British Columbia, reaches the sea at Vancouver and brings more fresh water on average than all of Puget Sound's rivers together, with a great flood of snowmelt from late May into July. Its water spreads across the Strait of Georgia and works south and west through the San Juan Islands to the Strait of Juan de Fuca, where it heads out to the Pacific on top. On the way it mixes with the salty water below, and some of that mixed water is drawn back east in the Strait's deep inflow and through Admiralty Inlet into the Sound. No one in Seattle sees the Fraser's water as such, but it freshens the whole system.

blocks.caption: The Salish Sea's two-layer exchange. Solid blue lines: fresher water flowing out on top, from the Main Basin and from the Fraser, toward the Pacific. Dashed dark blue line: ocean water flowing in below, from the Pacific to the Main Basin. Pale area: summer upwelling on the outer coast.

blocks.text: If that were all, the Sound would be layered like a summer lake: a warm, fresh skin on top and cold salt water below, holding apart. It isn't, because of the sills. At Admiralty Inlet the floor rises so that the deepest channel over the sill is only about 60 metres deep, between the deep water of the Strait and the deep Main Basin behind it. Twice a day the tide drags all of that water over the rise, top to bottom, at a few knots (lesson 11), and it tumbles and churns as it goes. The two layers are stirred into each other. Tacoma Narrows, at the entrance to South Sound, does the same.

Much of the fresher water heading out on top never makes it to the Strait. It is mixed down at the sill into the salty water below and carried straight back into the Sound with the inflow. Oceanographers call this **reflux**, and their estimates for Admiralty Inlet put it at roughly half or more of the outflowing water.

Stirring is also what keeps the surface cold. **An estimate.** Energy is counted in joules; a watt is one joule each second. In July the sunlight reaching the Sound averages about 250 watts on each square metre, counting day and night together. Over a week, 604,800 seconds, that is about 150 million joules on each square metre. Warming a cubic metre of water by one degree takes about 4 million joules. Kept in the top 5 metres, as in a calm lake, a week of sunshine could warm that layer by about 7 °C, before counting the heat the surface gives back to the air and sky. Stirred through the full 60 metres over the sill, the same heat warms the whole column by about half a degree. The sill takes the summer's heat and spreads it too thin for the surface to warm the way a lake does.

The tide flowing over the sills does one more thing. The boundary between the two layers carries waves of its own, called **internal waves**, and the sills make them. A wave on the surface is pulled back toward level by the full weight of the water against air. A wave on the boundary inside the water is pulled back only by the difference in weight between the two layers, a few percent, so it is slow and can be tall, rising and falling many metres while the surface above barely moves. Groups of them march away from the sills across the Main Basin.

You can see them on a calm day without seeing them. Look out over the Sound from a ferry or a high bluff and you may see long, smooth bands lying across the rippled water, parallel to one another, sometimes a few hundred metres apart. Each band is a **slick**. As an internal wave passes, the water above it is pushed forward over some parts of the wave and drawn back over others, so the surface water is squeezed together in a band above each wave. The squeeze gathers the thin natural films that lie on the water, and the films smooth out the ripples. The slicks drift along with the waves beneath them.

blocks.caption: Internal waves on the boundary between the two layers, and the slicks they make on the surface. Not to scale: the internal waves are many metres tall and hundreds of metres long.

blocks.text: The deep water of the Main Basin is replaced from time to time by new water from the Strait. The new water has to be heavy enough to sink all the way to the bottom, and whether it is depends on how much fresher water the sill has mixed into it on the way in. In a study published in 1982, W. Rockwell Geyer and Glenn Cannon showed from measurements at the sill and in the basin that the new deep water arrives in pulses, about twice a month.

The figure below is a model of what they found. Its top half is a slice along the Sound: the Strait on the left, the sill, and the Main Basin on the right, with the outflow on top, the inflow below, swirls of mixing at the sill and an arrow showing the share of the outflow carried back in. A pulse is when the inflow arrow dives all the way to the floor of the basin. Below the slice, a purple strip shows the strength of the tidal currents, high at spring tides and low at neaps, and a chart compares the density of the water crossing the sill (solid) with that of the bottom water (dashed); a pulse shades the chart. A slider sets the rivers' flow. Before the controls unlock, the figure asks whether the pulses come at spring tides or at neaps.

blocks.caption: A month of exchange at the Admiralty Inlet sill. A model: salt alone sets the density, and the mixing at the sill grows with the strength of the tidal current.

blocks.text: The pulses come at **neap tides**, the weak tides of lesson 8, and stop at springs. It seems backward at first: the strong tides move the most water, so surely they should deliver the most. But at springs the fast currents over the sill stir hard, much of the outgoing fresher water is mixed into the inflow, and the inflow arrives lighter than the water already at the bottom of the basin. It can't sink through heavier water, so it spreads out at the depth where it fits, partway down. At neaps the stirring slackens, the inflow keeps more of its salt, and it is the heaviest water around. It slides down the far side of the sill and along the floor of the basin, lifting the older bottom water ahead of it.

Move the river slider and the details shift: more river water makes the surface layer fresher, the inflow a little lighter and the whole Sound a little less salty. The timing of the pulses stays the same. The rivers rise and fall over weeks and months, and they freshen the inflow and the bottom water alike, while the tide's strength swings from strong to weak and back every two weeks. That swing is what moves the inflow above and below the bottom water's density, so renewal keeps the rhythm of the springs and neaps.

Stirring explains why the summer's heat spreads thin. The other half of the answer is what comes in. In spring and summer the winds along the outer coast of Washington blow mostly from the north, toward the south. Because of the Earth's spin, the surface water they push is turned to its right, and for water heading south the right is west: out to sea, away from the coast.[^ekman] Water from below rises to take its place: cold, salty water from a hundred metres or more down, rich in the nutrients that sank there over the years. This is **upwelling**, and it keeps the coastal water cold through the summer.

That upwelled water is the deep water that flows in along the bottom of the Strait of Juan de Fuca. All summer, the two-layer exchange draws cold ocean water from the coast into the Sound, while the sills stir it up to the surface. The cold you feel at Alki in July is partly water that was a hundred metres down off the outer coast not long before. Its nutrients also feed the plankton, tiny drifting algae, that turn the summer Sound green; they are the next course's subject.

The Sound is not cold everywhere. The cold depends on the stirring and the supply, and where both are weak the water warms. The long, shallow inlets of South Sound, Budd Inlet, Eld Inlet, Totten and Hammersley, lie far beyond Tacoma Narrows at the very end of the exchange, and in a warm summer their surface water reaches 18 to 20 °C. Hood Canal, the long arm of the Sound west of the Kitsap Peninsula, is closed at its southern end and has weak tidal currents. In summer it layers much as a lake does, with warm water on top; lesson 13 follows what happens beneath.

blocks.caption: Typical surface temperatures in late July, rounded; each bar is drawn at the middle of its range. Each varies from year to year and day to day.

parts.title: A wedge in the river mouth

blocks.text: The two layers can hold apart where little stirs them. At the mouth of a river that enters through a narrow, dredged channel, the Duwamish Waterway through Seattle's industrial district for one, salt water pushes upstream along the bottom as a thin, tapering layer under the fresh water flowing out on top. This is a **salt wedge**. Its front, where it thins to nothing on the riverbed, is called the toe, and it can be several kilometres from the mouth. The heavy salt water would creep all the way upstream if nothing held it back; what holds it back is the river, dragging on the top of the wedge as it flows out over it. In the figure below, the slider sets the river's flow in cubic metres a second: a strong river pushes the wedge back toward the sea, and a weak one lets it in.

blocks.caption: A salt wedge in a river channel 10 metres deep, held back by the river's flow. A model of a wedge with no tide; a real wedge also moves in and out with the tide.
blocks.task: Find a river flow that lets the salt reach at least 6 km upstream, then a high flow that pushes it back within 1 km

blocks.text: The best-known wedge in Seattle is one people made. The Ballard Locks, opened in 1917, lift ships from the salt water of Salmon Bay to the fresh water of the Lake Washington Ship Canal and Lake Union. Every time the large lock opens to the canal it lets out a lock full of salt water, which slides along the canal bed toward Lake Union like a wedge with no river strong enough to stop it. Left alone, the salt would build up in the bottom of Lake Union and beyond. The engineers' answer uses the same physics as the glass in the kitchen: salt water lies on the bottom, so it can be caught there. A barrier on the floor of the large lock holds much of it back, and a drain in the canal bed just above the locks collects salt water that gets past and pipes it back to Salmon Bay below the locks. The Seattle branch (S2) tells the story of the locks.

blocks.caption: The Ballard Locks from the side, not to scale. Salt water that gets past the large lock slides along the bottom of the canal and is caught by a drain.
Six questions on the Sound's layers
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Why does river water spread over the top of the salt water in Puget Sound?
choices: River water is warmer than the Sound in most months, and warm water floats on cold
River water holds almost no salt, which makes it lighter by more than temperature can
River water arrives moving fast, and its speed carries it over the slower sea water
items.why: Sea water in the Sound is 2 to 3 percent denser than river water, while temperature changes density by only a few tenths of a percent.

items.ask: Why does ocean water flow into Puget Sound along the bottom all year?
choices: The surface outflow carries salt away, and a salty inflow below must replace it
The flood tide runs longer near the bottom than the ebb does, so water collects there
The weight of the rivers pushes the surface down, forcing ocean water in underneath
items.why: Outflow on top takes salt away; the salt is kept by an inflow of salty water underneath, many times the rivers' flow.

items.ask: What is reflux at the Admiralty Inlet sill?
choices: Ocean water that enters on the flood and leaves again on the next ebb, unmixed
Deep water that rises over the sill and spills back out into the Strait
Outgoing surface water that is mixed down at the sill and carried back in
items.why: Tidal stirring over the sill mixes the layers, so much of the water leaving on top is returned in the inflow below.

items.ask: Why does new deep water reach the bottom of the Main Basin at neap tides rather than at springs?
choices: Neap tides carry more water over the sill each day than spring tides do
Weak neap currents mix less fresh water into the inflow, so it stays heavy enough to sink
At neaps the outflow on top pauses, so the inflow meets no fresher water at all
items.why: At springs hard stirring lightens the inflow so it spreads at mid-depth; at neaps it keeps more of its salt and sinks to the floor.

items.ask: Which best explains why the Main Basin stays near 12 to 14 °C in summer?
choices: Snowmelt rivers keep pouring near-freezing water into the Sound right through summer
Fog and low cloud over the Sound in July keep most of the sun's heat from reaching it
Stirring spreads the sun's heat through deep water while cold upwelled water flows in
items.why: The sun's heat is mixed down through the full depth at the sills, and the summer inflow is cold water brought up along the coast by north winds.

items.ask: In a river mouth with a salt wedge, what happens to the wedge when the river runs high?
choices: It is pushed back toward the sea, because the faster river drags harder on it
It moves further upstream, because high water brings more of the sea in with it
It stays where it is, because salt water is heavier than anything the river moves
items.why: The wedge creeps upstream along the bottom until the river's drag holds it back; a stronger river holds it nearer the mouth.

wilkes.title: Wilkes's names
wilkes.text: Wilkes's expedition named many places on the Sound that still carry the names, among them Elliott Bay and Commencement Bay.

knudsen.title: Knudsen's balance
knudsen.text: The Danish oceanographer Martin Knudsen wrote down this salt and water balance in 1900, for the Baltic. It gives the size of an estuary's exchange from two salinities and the river flow, without measuring the currents at all.

ekman.title: Turned to the right
ekman.text: In the Northern Hemisphere the Earth's spin turns moving water to the right. Averaged through the wind-driven surface layer, the water moves at right angles to the wind, as Vagn Walfrid Ekman worked out in 1905. A north wind on the Washington coast blows toward the south, so the water moves west, out to sea.

density.title: Salt and temperature together
density.text: Sea water's density depends on salt, temperature and pressure together. Each extra gram of salt per kilogram adds about 0.8 kilograms to a cubic metre, while each degree of warming takes off only about 0.1 to 0.2, depending on the temperature. The sill figure in this lesson uses salt alone.
